author: Simon Innes
headline: Category & Procurement Strategy | Capital Projects | Real Estate Development | Energy & Renewables | UAE
text:
Saudi capital focus is shifting from giga projects to AI.

Giga project awards fell from about $34bn in 2023 to $14.3bn in 2025. In September, works for a planned 6 GW AI data centre campus in Riyadh were awarded, and Saudi Energy signed three deals to power data and AI centres.

This fits the narrative that capital is following AI into grid and generation. Saudi Energy's transmission spend went from SAR 10.1bn in 2023 to SAR 43.6bn in 2025.

The bigger question is the execution model. On one 100MW AI data centre tender, the owner supplies the backup generators and the EPC installs them. Are EPCs now mainly procuring the product? And are we moving to buy-or-build?

From a procurement seat:
- Long-lead kit (transformers, switchgear, UPS) sets the programme.
- Decide who buys it, owner or EPC, before the tender goes out.

We're asking this a lot at Efficio. Where do you see it going?

📊 #100DaysWithTVS | Week 16: Valuation Made Simple
Why is the market willing to pay a premium for Blue Dart Express?
In equity research, a company's share price tells us what investors are paying. Its P/E ratio helps us understand how much they are paying relative to its earnings.
Blue Dart Express operates an integrated air and ground transportation network, delivering time-sensitive shipments across India and beyond.
According to Screener, Blue Dart's P/E was approximately 34.1x as of October 2026.
In simple terms, investors were paying approximately ₹34 for every ₹1 of annual earnings.
But what could justify this valuation?
🔹 Established brand: Trust and reliability matter when customers need time-sensitive deliveries.
🔹 Integrated network: Its air and ground infrastructure supports end-to-end shipment delivery.
🔹 Profitability: The company reported a return on equity of approximately 14.7% and return on capital employed of 17.3%.
🔹 Growth potential: E-commerce, business shipments and demand for faster deliveries could support future growth.
However, there is another side to the story.
Blue Dart's five-year sales CAGR was approximately 13%, while its three-year sales CAGR was around 6%. Its three-year profit CAGR was approximately -10%.
This raises an important question: Is the premium valuation justified by the company's competitive strengths, or are investors expecting stronger future growth than recent results suggest?

National Power Construction Corporation (NPCC), a privatised power-sector company, has sought government approval to sell its remaining 12 percent government-owned shares to an existing majority shareholder, citing administrative, banking and regulatory hurdles affecting its business operations in Saudi Arabia.

According to sources in the Privatisation Division, NPCC Chief Executive Officer Muhammad Ajaz Malik has written to the government, seeking approval for the sale of the shares in accordance with the applicable legal framework and prescribed procedures.

The request follows the reversion of 12 percent shares, previously allocated under the Benazir Employees’ Stock Option Scheme (BESOS), to the Government of Pakistan after the Supreme Court declared the scheme unconstitutional.

NPCC was privatised with effect from December 1, 2015, through a competitive process conducted by the Privatisation Commission. Under the transaction, 88 percent of the shares owned by the President of Pakistan were sold to Saudi Arabia-based Mansour Al Mosaid Company for Trading and Contracting, along with the transfer of management control, following approval by the Cabinet Committee on Privatisation (CCoP).

The remaining 12 percent stake was allocated under BESOS and held through the Employees Empowerment Trust.

Brookfield and KKR are competing for a controlling stake in eyewa at a reported $700 million valuation.

The Riyadh- and Dubai-headquartered eyewear retailer has grown from an online business into a regional chain operating approximately 250 stores across the Gulf.

According to the Financial Times, both investment firms are frontrunners in advanced discussions. 
However, the deal is not confirmed and remains dependent on regional conditions.

The backdrop is what makes this interesting. Founded in 2017 by former Bain consultants Anass Boumediene, Mehdi Oudghiri and Abdullah AlRugaib, 
eyewa raised $100 million in November 2024 through a Series C led by General Atlantic, with participation from Badwa Capital and Turmeric Capital.

Earlier investors included Nuwa Capital, @Kingsway Capital, Wamda Capital and EQ2 Ventures.

The funding brought its disclosed total to approximately $130 million. By its last major fundraising, Eyewa's proprietary brands accounted for 96% of revenue, alongside a network of around 150 stores.

Brookfield, backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund for its Middle East buyout fund, and KKR, which has deployed around $5 billion in regional equity capital since January 2025, are both expanding their regional exposure.

Is Eyewa's potential $700 million deal another signal of global private equity's growing appetite for the Gulf's consumer market?

author: Alnilam Partners
headline: 24 followers
text:
Private school operators in the Gulf currently face a widening disconnect between student enrollment and net profitability because tuition pricing has shifted from local discretion to strict regulatory oversight. In Dubai, school capacity continues to expand while fee growth remains constrained, which forces operators to absorb rising operating costs. Internal analysis shows that holding utilization flat at 85 percent while freezing fees and inflating staff costs by 5 percent annually causes EBITDA to drop by 26 percent. This sensitivity explains why institutional investors must model maintainable EBITDA instead of relying on historical performance or standard market multiples.

Margin compression occurs because fixed costs like rent and teacher salaries do not scale down when fee increases are denied. When an operator faces a 26 percent EBITDA decline from a cost-price mismatch, the underlying asset value erodes quite rapidly. This reality forces a shift in acquisition strategy where entry multiples must be disciplined to account for regulatory risk. Paying 9x or 10x EBITDA for a mid-market school becomes dangerous if the revenue line is effectively capped by a regulator that prioritizes affordability over operator returns.

Acquirers should focus on mid-market assets with stable occupancy and conservative fee assumptions rather than chasing premium growth stories.

#gcc #education #privateequity

text:
📍 FOR INVESTORS

💡 In the GCC, localisation is a product feature.

A product that wins in London or Bangalore does not automatically win in Riyadh or Dubai. Too many investment memos treat localisation as a line item. It is a product decision.

Four questions to put to any company selling into the Gulf:

— Is Arabic designed in, or bolted on? Right-to-left layouts, Arabic search and Arabic-speaking support change adoption, especially in government and consumer markets.

— Where does the data live? Data-protection and residency expectations in Saudi Arabia and the UAE are a real factor in enterprise and public-sector deals. Ask early.

— Does it fit local payments and processes? Local payment methods, e-invoicing requirements, the regional working week.

— Is someone on the ground? Buyers here want to meet the people they are trusting.

💡 Companies that get this right build a moat that global competitors find hard to cross. Companies that ignore it tend to stall at the pilot stage.

Investors: which localisation gap have you seen stall a deal?

#VentureCapital #GCC #SaudiArabia #UAE #Localisation #TechInvestment #AbornOne

text:

For years, the Gulf-and-America story was mostly sovereign wealth: late-stage money flying into US tech from Abu Dhabi and Riyadh. That is still happening. What has changed is who is writing the earlier cheques.

A new generation of Gulf venture funds has just raised, or just doubled, and they are deploying. Some of that money is staying in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Riyadh. Some of it is already landing on founders in the United States.

text:
THE GCC’S NEXT DEALMAKING FRONTIER: FROM CAPITAL SOURCE TO INVESTMENT DESTINATION

Global investors have long viewed the Gulf primarily as a source of capital.

Now, will they increasingly invest in the region’s own companies?

Two recent developments stand out.

EY reported on November 11 that MENA recorded 572 M&A transactions worth $83.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 21% in value year-on-year. Outbound deals reached $57.5 billion, while inbound deals totaled just $3.4 billion.

On November 15, the Financial Times reported that Brookfield and KKR were competing for a controlling stake in Gulf eyewear retailer Eyewa, in talks that could value the business at approximately $700 million. The transaction remains under discussion.

The strategic question: Can the GCC evolve from a global capital exporter into a deeper destination for institutional buyouts?

1 | FROM SOVEREIGN DEALS TO SCALABLE COMPANIES

Government-related entities participated in deals representing 77% of MENA’s total M&A value in the first nine months of 2026, according to EY.

Sovereign capital remains pivotal. But the next stage requires more privately owned, institutionally managed businesses capable of attracting international investors on their own merits.

2 | THE MIDDLE MARKET MAY BE THE REAL OPPORTUNITY

author: Michael Mudau
headline: COO @ Sharp Minds | ex-Bain | INSEAD
text:
I was shocked when I found out how fast a Gulf cabinet decision becomes a live tender. 

If you run a programme here, here's what it means for you.

A government decision taken in April was within a live tender in a few weeks. Your hiring plan probably wasn't built for that clock.

You're likely building something that didn't exist last year: a bank, an insurer, a national data platform. 

You need people who’ve built that thing before. And while you need them for the build, you may not need them for the decade after.

A permanent senior hire means a search, a notice period and often a relocation. By then, your programme’s timelines are squeezing you.

ُHerein lies the benefit of hiring fractional experts. 

That said, fractional may not suit every role. If the job is permanent and core, hire full time. If it's a build, the maths points the other way.

Before you sign off 2027 headcount, ask: which of these roles are permanent, and which are really a build?

—

I’m Michael Mudau, COO at Sharp Minds. I help GCC programme leaders bring in senior ex-consultants for the build, with three profiles in 48 hours.

author: Jellyn Lasala
headline: Investment Associate- Deal Scout
text:
Venture capital isn’t experiencing a drought—it’s experiencing extreme concentration.
While headlines often focus on how tough fundraising has become for early-stage founders, total capital deployment tells a very different story. Through Q3 2026, AI alone captured over 80% of all venture capital dollars, driven by unprecedented mega-rounds for foundational infrastructure and compute.   
For founders and operators, the market has split into two distinct realities:
The Mega-Round Tier: Massive funds are writing massive checks for category-defining AI, sovereign infrastructure, and deep tech.   
The Disciplined Core: For everyone else, the era of "growth at all costs" is permanently over. Capital efficiency, clear unit economics, and vertical-specific moats are the new baseline for raising a round.   
Meanwhile, companies are staying private longer, shifting focus toward strategic M&A and a more selective IPO window as the primary paths to liquidity.   
Are you seeing the same bifurcation in your sector right now?

Currently serving as Chairman of Miza Capital since February 2025 and as a Board Member at WalaPlus since January 2024, Moath previously served as CEO of Alfanar Capital and as CEO & Managing Director of Yaqeen Capital for over eight years, where he also served as Chairman of Mutual Funds and Managing Director of Investment Banking. Earlier in his career, he served as Manager of Investment Banking at Yaqeen Capital and as a Board Member at Alamthal Finance.

Moath has successfully executed numerous deals, including over 50 IPOs — a remarkable track record that reflects his deep expertise in capital markets, transaction management, and regulatory navigation.

Moath holds a Master of Business Administration (MBA) from Dalhousie University and has completed executive education in Private Equity & Venture Capital at Harvard Business School. He brings 20 skills to his work, including Risk Management and Investment Banking, with strong endorsements from peers.
